articles.title: Here are the brands bringing ads to ChatGPT
articles.summary: OpenAI has launched its advertising pilot in ChatGPT, and several brands, including Target, Audible, Adobe, and others, have announced plans to participate.
articles.body: OpenAI officially launched its advertising pilot in ChatGPT, leaving us with a better idea of the kinds of products we might see stuffed beneath our conversations with the AI chatbot. Several companies have announced plans to show ads inside ChatGPT — placements that will reportedly cost them a pretty penny — ranging from major retailers like Target to automakers like Ford and Mazda. You’ll only see ads in ChatGPT if you’re a free user or subscribed to its cheaper $8 / month Go plan. OpenAI has said it will “clearly” label the ads and that they won’t influence ChatGPT’s response. Here are all the brands that we know are partnering with OpenAI so far. Target Target says in an announcement that it will use ads in ChatGPT to help users “discover products, deals and inspiration that meet what they’re seeking at that moment.” It notes that ads will appear based on keywords that appear in a user’s ChatGPT prompt. As an example, Target says someone using ChatGPT to look for “countertop cooking appliances that make everyday meals more convenient” might see an ad for an air fryer from Target. Adobe Adobe is planning to show ads for its AI-powered document editor, Acrobat Studio, and its AI video and image generator, Adobe Firefly, in ChatGPT. It’s positioning the partnership as a way to “better understand how ads can provide helpful, relevant experiences” as it ramps up its own platform designed to help advertisers show up in AI search results. Williams-Sonoma You might see ads for Williams-Sonoma’s range of housewares, kitchenware, furniture, and other products, too. The company says it’s going to explore how ads in ChatGPT will help “surface relevant, high-quality products” at “decision-making moments.” Audible It looks like ChatGPT’s ads won’t be limited to tangible products, either, as the Amazon-owned Audible plans to work with OpenAI to “reach new audiobook listeners” through ChatGPT. It’s not clear whether Audible will only show ads for its subscription or if it will showcase specific audiobooks when someone asks ChatGPT for recommendations. HelloFresh The meal kit company HelloFresh is also bringing ads to ChatGPT. Patrick Stal, the company’s senior vice president of global marketing, says on LinkedIn that the partnership will allow the brand to offer a “solution” to customers using ChatGPT for things like meal planning. Ford, Mazda, Mrs. Myers, and more The advertising agency WPP Media is working with Ford, Mazda, the cleaning company Mrs. Myers, and the luxury Swiss watch company Audemars Piguet to launch ads in ChatGPT as well. (Its other clients include Audible and Adobe, too). Meanwhile, other agencies, including Dentsu and Omnicom, have announced that they’re going to bring their clients’ ads to ChatGPT as well, though they don’t specify which brands are involved. Instead, Dentsu notes that it has “several clients” participating in OpenAI’s test across grocery, hospitality, retail, software, travel, and the consumer packaged goods (CPG) industries, which could include items like food and beverages, cosmetics, or cleaning products. Omnicom lists companies specializing in apparel, automotive, beauty, CPG, technology, telecommunications, hospitality, retail, and fast-food as participants in OpenAI’s test. Update, February 11th: Added HelloFresh.

articles.title: IAs da OpenAI enfraquecem sistema criado para monitorá-las | G1
articles.standfirst: Em um dos casos, modelo retirou um mecanismo de segurança e depois afirmou incorretamente que não havia feito isso.
articles.summary: Em um dos casos, modelo retirou um mecanismo de segurança e depois afirmou incorretamente que não havia feito isso.
articles.body:
As preocupações que levaram a OpenAI, do ChatGPT, a abandonar lançamento de novo sistema de IA — Foto: Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images

A OpenAI informou que dois de seus agentes de inteligência artificial (IA) enfraqueceram sistemas de segurança usados pela empresa para monitorar as ações dos próprios modelos. Os casos ocorreram durante tarefas internas de programação.

Esse é o caso mais recente de agentes de IA que agiram de maneiras não previstas por seus desenvolvedores.

Embora a empresa responsável pelo ChatGPT tenha afirmado que os incidentes ocorreram durante tarefas internas de programação e não foram classificados entre os casos mais graves, os episódios mostram que até os sistemas criados para detectar comportamentos inadequados da IA podem sofrer interferência dos próprios agentes que monitoram.

A revelação ocorre em meio a preocupações crescentes de que os avanços na segurança da IA não acompanhem o ritmo de desenvolvimento de sistemas cada vez mais poderosos. Pesquisadores têm alertado que agentes avançados podem se tornar mais difíceis de monitorar e controlar à medida que ganham autonomia.

Empresas como OpenAI e Anthropic, rivais que se preparam para abrir o capital, revelaram nos últimos meses casos em que agentes de IA acessaram sistemas externos sem autorização.

Em 3 de outubro, um agente GPT-6.1 Sol que realizava um teste interno desativou alertas automáticos de segurança após interpretar que uma instrução anterior para não enviar mensagens pelo Slack também se aplicava às notificações de segurança, segundo a OpenAI.

Em outro episódio, em 6 de outubro, um agente GPT-6 Astra removeu um mecanismo de monitoramento de segurança enquanto copiava um código existente e depois afirmou, incorretamente, que não havia feito isso, segundo a OpenAI.

“Em ambos os casos, os agentes avaliaram se os mecanismos de monitoramento deveriam ser mantidos, mas interpretaram instruções rotineiras de programação como permissão para enfraquecê-los”, afirmou a empresa.

A OpenAI afirmou que está adotando medidas para dificultar que os modelos desativem os mecanismos de monitoramento, mas admitiu que “ainda não tem uma explicação satisfatória para esse comportamento”.

A empresa também está investigando se seus modelos podem ter uma tendência a evitar o monitoramento e buscar justificativas para fazer isso.

articles.title: Conversational Gemini navigation comes to Apple CarPlay
articles.summary: After introducing its Gemini AI assistant to Android Auto last year, Google is now bringing it to Apple CarPlay users.
articles.body: After introducing its Gemini AI assistant to Android Auto last year, Google is now bringing it to Apple CarPlay users. The conversational Gemini in navigation is available today for US drivers, with “rollout happening globally too,” according to Google (we’ve asked for specific regional availability details). It’s taken almost 12 months for Google to bring this to CarPlay users, but now they can talk to the voice assistant in Google Maps to get some hands-free help while driving. That includes asking it multi-step questions, such as recommendations on places to visit and then prompting it to direct you there while avoiding toll roads. Users can activate the feature by tapping the Gemini icon in Google Maps on their Car’s infotainment display. Google describes this CarPlay support update as a conversational way to report traffic disruptions and find information about stops and places on-the-go. There’s no mention of any of the Personal Intelligence features that were announced yesterday for Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in, however, which enable the voice assistant to access user information from Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search. We’ve asked Google if CarPlay users will also receive the personalization update and will update if we hear back.

articles.title: Who's paying for the AI build-out? Probably you
articles.summary: What was the cost of the Great Pyramid of Giza, as a percentage of the Fourth Dynasty's GDP? It is unlikely that Pharaoh Khufu thought in those...
articles.body:
What was the cost of the Great Pyramid of Giza, as a percentage of the Fourth Dynasty's GDP? It is unlikely that Pharaoh Khufu thought in those terms, and the accounts have been lost over the intervening 4,600 years. The question is topical nonetheless, as America is building a 21st-century equivalent: an AI data centre network that dwarfs all of its previous infrastructure efforts.

Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of Brookings estimates the AI infrastructure boom will cost the equivalent of 3.6 per cent of US GDP a year over the eight-year period ending in 2032 — equalling the annual spending on the railroad boom of the late 19th century, plus the interstate highway projects of the mid-20th century, plus about two-thirds of the electrification spending of the early 20th century. Total bill: $10.3tn, an estimate including only tangible expenditures, not intangibles such as software.

Who pays? Substantially all of the profits of some of the world's most profitable companies — the so-called hyperscalers — have been staked. Add to this the new debt these mega-companies are taking on directly or guaranteeing, supplemented by more speculative debt and equity financing for smaller companies. Almost every big pool of capital, from every corner of the developed world, has been tapped. In short, if you have invested savings, you are financing the AI build-out.

The details are not easy to nail down, but hyperscalers' direct investments are the most transparent. Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle and SpaceX are expected to generate $760bn in cash flow this year. All of this and more will be invested, meaning "free cash flow" will be negative, a situation Wall Street expects to persist for several years, even as profits at the companies are projected to grow at a breakneck 30 per cent a year.

Equity investors can console themselves with the idea that a big chunk of the hyperscalers' investment converts into profits at semiconductor companies. But remember that these companies are investing heavily, too: capital expenditures at the 30 largest are set to pass $200bn this year, double the level of three years ago, and to grow from there.

There is another layer of financing flowing from the hyperscalers and chipmakers: equity investments in AI labs and other AI start-ups. Nvidia, for example, carries $94bn in private and public equity investments on its balance sheet, including stakes in OpenAI, Anthropic and CoreWeave. In a gold rush, it is often said, the real profits are made selling picks and shovels. In the AI gold rush, the shovel companies are investing part of their profits to buy mines.

articles.title: Decades-old flaw in PHP discovered by Google, OpenAI AI tools forces government and public websites to go offline globally
articles.summary: Government portals, municipal networks and public institutions across Europe and other regions went offline on Wednesday (October 21) after researchers
articles.body: Government portals, municipal networks and public institutions across Europe and other regions went offline on Wednesday (October 21) after researchers disclosed critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a foundational programming language that powers a vast portion of the global web. The disclosures prompted emergency responses from IT teams worldwide, with operators taking critical servers offline as a defensive shield to prevent malicious intrusions before security updates could be deployed. Developers of the open-source PHP language published urgent security fixes for flaws that had remained buried inside the language’s codebase for years. Issuing an emergency advisory, the team stated that all site owners and server administrators are “encouraged to update immediately.”With tech security firms warning that malicious actors have already begun targeting unpatched setups, the disclosure triggered an immediate “race to exploit.” As fixes are now public, analysts warned that artificial intelligence (AI) tools could allow hackers to reverse-engineer the vulnerability with minimal effort.“Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale. With AI this is no longer a barrier,” noted cybersecurity firm Wiz, warning that AI-assisted attacks could lead to the mass compromise of unprotected web servers across the internet.Flaw impacting the ‘backbone of the web’Created in the early 1990s as “Personal Home Page,” PHP has evolved into one of the core backbones of modern internet infrastructure. When a user visits a webpage, servers running PHP assemble the text, media and code before serving it to the browser. According to web analytics tracker W3Techs, PHP underpins roughly 75% of all websites where the server-side language can be identified.“All servers using any version of PHP released in the last 20 years will be vulnerable. This issue impacts the majority of the Internet,” said Tiffany Farriss, interim chief executive of the Drupal Association.Due to this widespread footprint, national cyber agencies across Britain, Europe, Japan and Australia issued advisories directing web administrators to install updates immediately or take public-facing pages offline.Flaw discovered through Artificial IntelligenceThe underlying security flaw sat hidden in the software codebase for over a decade. In a technical brief, Alphabet-owned cybersecurity firm Wiz revealed that human researchers would have found it extraordinarily complex to locate and exploit through conventional testing. Instead, the vulnerability was surfaced through advanced AI tooling:Wiz discovered the flaw using Wiz Atlas, its autonomous vulnerability discovery system, working alongside Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. Wiz collaborated with the PHP core developer team, OpenAI and security firm Calif to verify the bug and confirm remediation patches.Early mitigation protocols were shared with cloud and infrastructure operators, including Google Cloud, Cloudflare, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft, Automattic (operator of WordPress.com), Fastly, Akamai, Imperva and Vercel.You use AI every day. articles.title: PHP armageddon: OpenAI, Google's Wiz find ancient holes, panicking the internet | TechCrunch
articles.summary: This is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented by AI, but is also a high risk because of AI.
articles.body:
The U.S. National Security Agency’s sent out an alarming warning on Wednesday that two critical holes had been found in PHP, with patches already issued by the PHP Foundation .

PHP is a server-side programming language so widely used for web applications that it powers roughly 70% of the websites on the internet; by some accounts, that’s more than 33 million sites . It is also used by popular content management systems like WordPress.

The NSA warned that these holes are so severe that if a website can’t be patched immediately, it should be pulled off the web until it can be. The holes allow attackers to infiltrate the server’s file system or a database that may be used by the web app.

Interestingly, these holes have been tucked away in all versions of PHP since version 5, which was released in 2004. Websites not running relatively current versions of PHP will have some updating work to do, as PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported. The recommendation is to update the web server to the current version of PHP, which is 8.5.12.

So how did two such ubiquitous, decades-old flaws that affect nearly every website on the internet suddenly come to light? AI, naturally, particularly via OpenAI and Google’s Wiz.

Security testing company Calif was engaged in OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative to find flaws in open-source source software. Using GPT‑5.6 Sol, it found one of the flaws, OpenAI disclosed in a blog post . Separately, the Wiz team also used AI, namely its Wiz Atlas security AI agent, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to find multiple vulnerabilities in PHP.

Both OpenAI and Wiz followed responsible security research practices and worked with PHP on patches before publicly disclosing the flaws. Then they all worked together to flesh out what they found, and test the patches, drawing in a host of others to help.

Wiz thanked Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Imperva, Microsoft, and Vercel. (While WordPress sites use PHP, WordPress has issued a statement saying that the flaw isn’t WordPress specific, and sites running its CMS must patch their servers and work with their web-hosting companies to ensure their sites are protected.)

OpenAI says that these flaws were found by researchers before hackers discovered them. So there were no reports of exploits in the wild. This is also in part because, before AI, these flaws were too hard for hackers to exploit. “With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts,” Wiz warned in its blog about the flaws.

In other words, this is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented because of AI, but is also a high risk only because of AI.

Now that the issue has been disclosed, hackers are fully in the know. The race is on for the internet to patch tens millions of websites before hackers can attack the unpatched ones. Hence the NSA’s guidance that if you can’t patch your PHP website right away, you’re better off pulling it offline until you can.

articles.title: GM is giving OnStar an AI makeover
articles.summary: It's one of the biggest overhauls ever to the 30-year-old connected car product.
articles.body:
General Motors is adding a personal AI assistant to OnStar as part of a broader makeover of the subscription-based connected car service that the U.S. automaker launched 30 years ago.

The OnStar AI Assistant will debut in the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV in the coming months, with more GM vehicles to follow, the company said Wednesday at its GM Forward event in New York, where it made a series of other technology announcements covering software, automated driving, EVs, and its electrical architecture. The company said it will launch a new OnStar mobile app in 2027 that will complement and sync up with its in-car software.

The new OnStar mobile app will replace the current OnStar Guardian app that launched in 2020 as well as vehicle brand apps for Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC.

This tech-centric reboot is unlike other attempts to modernize OnStar and it notably puts agentic AI at the center. The company has updated the safety and roadside assistance service numerous times in its history, especially in the past five years as it tried to stay apace of emerging and tech-forward competitors like Tesla.

In 2021, the company expanded its OnStar Guardian app, which offered crash detection, emergency assistance and location sharing, to anyone with a compatible phone, even if they didn’t own a GM vehicle. A year later, GM started using Google Cloud’s conversational AI Dialogflow to recognize specific spoken requests and expanded in 2023 to give drivers responses to common queries like routing and navigation assistance — all part of GM’s plan to build a $25 billion subscription business by 2030 .

GM continued to focus on generative AI, but relied on Google to provide the experience. The company said last year that Google Gemini would roll out in vehicles in 2026.

The OnStar AI Assistant is an in-house effort and one aimed at giving the driver and passengers an interactive and custom experience — and become even more embedded in their daily lives.

“OnStar is now transitioning to be a connected intelligence platform, not just the call center that it’s historically been known as, but a mechanism for interpreting, understanding, and providing predictive, proactive support to its owners,” GM’s VP of global product and chief product officer Sterling Anderson told TechCrunch in an interview ahead of the GM Forward event.

For instance, cameras on the vehicle will be connected to the software to offer live views as well as crash and safety recordings. Users can set up the connected cameras to turn on automatically if the vehicle senses an impending event — for instance an aggressive horn honk — then capture the event and upload it to the OnStar app. Users will be able to use voice to control certain functions on the vehicle, including climate, and ask questions about any specific vehicle feature.

The launch coincides with efforts throughout the auto industry to stay apace of Chinese automakers with technology that is central to the vehicle — and no longer a slapped on gimmick or feature. But that has required GM to change its approach to software development, adopt AI tools, and even design a new electrical and centralized compute vehicle architecture.

The announcement also comes after GM has been criticized and even fined for sharing data with third parties. Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission finalized an order that bans General Motors and its OnStar telematics service from sharing certain consumer data with consumer reporting agencies. The finalized order also requires the automaker to be more transparent with its consumers and obtain their explicit consent on certain data collection.

GM said Wednesday that customers will have the ability to decide what data is shared, and that the recordings have time limits and are encrypted. GM said it and OnStar cannot access Connected Camera recordings.

A GM spokesperson later shared that third-party sharing a “feature-specific and consent-based, with information shared only as needed to provide requested functionality.” Customers can manage permissions and withdraw consent, however those who choose not to share certain data may have limited access to related features, while other OnStar services would continue, according to GM.

articles.title: GM taps AI to help match speed of Chinese rivals
articles.summary: General Motors wants to slash the time it takes to develop a new vehicle in half, betting that artificial intelligence can help it compete with China's much...
articles.body:
General Motors wants to slash the time it takes to develop a new vehicle in half, betting that artificial intelligence can help it compete with China's much faster automakers.

Why it matters: Chinese carmakers have a formidable speed advantage , allowing them to introduce new models and technologies faster than their Western rivals can respond.

The big picture: GM chief product officer Sterling Anderson acknowledges that Chinese automakers benefit from a deeply integrated supplier ecosystem that allows them to source common components quickly and efficiently.

Western automakers lack that advantage, he told Axios.

But he said GM has other advantages, including decades of accumulated engineering and manufacturing data it can leverage to accelerate development.

GM aims to leverage that data to shrink its traditional four-to-five-year vehicle development cycle to roughly two years by using AI and virtual engineering to streamline design, testing and manufacturing.

How it works: GM is using AI to replace what Anderson describes as slow, sequential engineering processes with faster, parallel development and virtual testing.

For example, engineers were able to evaluate more than 300,000 designs for GM's new lithium manganese-rich (LMR) batteries virtually before building a physical prototype.

That helped the team move from its first battery-pack concept to formal approval in just one month.

GM is also using its vast records of component designs, material properties and manufacturing instructions to build digital models of vehicles and factories, enabling engineers to test changes before implementing them in the real world.

Between the lines: GM's enormous scale has historically made it difficult to change direction quickly. But that same scale has generated a treasure trove of data that could become an advantage in the AI era.

"There is inertia in scale," Anderson acknowledged. But "with scale comes data."

The challenge now is turning that data into faster development cycles — and ultimately better vehicles.

"The faster you move, the more you iterate," Anderson tells Axios. "The more you iterate, the better the product gets."

The bottom line: GM isn't trying to copy China's manufacturing playbook. It's betting that AI can help it achieve similar speed through a different route.

articles.title: Walmart is inviting AI agents to shop for you
articles.summary: Walmart will soon let AI agents shop on the site for you. With new “Agent Profiles,” you’ll be able to review your agent’s purchases and set spending limits.
articles.body: Walmart will soon let AI agents shop on its website for you. Next month, the retail giant will allow you to use an AI agent on the site, with systems in place to let you approve and review purchases and set spending limits. The embrace of AI agents stands in stark contrast to Amazon, which blocked Perplexity’s shopping agent and Meta’s Muse AI assistant. But Walmart is opening its doors to AI shoppers — as long as they follow the retailer’s rules. It has outlined a set of terms for agents, saying that “agents must not take actions beyond what the shopper intends” and cannot change a customer’s payment method. Agents also can only access information needed to complete their task. Walmart says it will block agents that don’t follow these terms. [Image: Your AI agent will get its own profile within your Walmart account. Agents will connect to new “Agent Profiles” within Walmart. By default, Walmart will require approval for all AI agent purchases, but you can also let it shop within a certain budget, such as up to $100. You’ll also be able to review your agent’s purchases separately from your own in Agent Profiles, as well as turn off the agent at any time. The retailer has built an “Agent Gateway,” currently available in beta, that connects AI agents through the Model Context Protocol, an open standard that allows AI agents to plug into different services on the web. Walmart says this not only enables AI agents to shop without running into hiccups that they might encounter when navigating a browser, but also prevents them from accessing your shopping history and personal information. “For example, if a customer tends to buy sourdough bread or a particular brand of milk, Walmart will help the agent find those usual items for the customer without sharing the customer’s broader shopping history with the agent,” Walmart says. The company will let users shop with AI agents on Sam’s Club as well.

articles.title: While Amazon blocks AI agents, Walmart rolls out the welcome mat | TechCrunch
articles.summary: As Amazon blocks AI agents from shopping on its site, Walmart is taking the opposite approach, introducing new technology that lets AI agents make purchases on customers' behalf, with controls over spending and transaction approvals.
articles.body:
Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers.

The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely . Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others.

Now, it’s expanding on those efforts with more technology to prepare for a world where AI agents become mainstream, said Walmart President and CEO John Furner, speaking at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco on Wednesday. The technology will support agentic shopping from both Walmart and the company’s discount warehouse, Sam’s Club.

It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user.

What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent.

The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer, and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do.

With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set.

The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified, and you can cap their spending.

The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary.

Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent.

Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site.

articles.title: Anthropic takes on Muse with Claude Duet, its new AI agent
articles.summary: Anthropic just announced Claude Duet, an AI agent competitor to Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots that’s designed for professionals and small business owners. It’s available as a “research preview.”
articles.body: Anthropic just announced an AI agent competitor to Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots: Claude Duet. The new agent, designed for professionals and small business owners, is launching as a “research preview,” according to Anthropic, and it’s available as a standalone app on iOS and Android and through Claude on the web. The AI agent is built around Claude Opus 5.5. Here’s Anthropic’s description of what it can do: > Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps. Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention. You can also hand it tasks of all shapes—from simple administrative tasks of scheduling meetings to more complex ones, such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps. Claude Duet pulls in memory, skills, and connected apps from Claude, and it has a virtual machine with a browser that it can use for completing work. Before any big step, like sending a payment or deleting something, Claude Duet messages you for approval. Given that Duet may be taking action on sensitive information, it has a new “new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt” that are “designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information,” such as credit card numbers. Anthropic says Claude Duet is currently an “early version” and that it “still might misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent.” It’s also not “as strong” at personal errands like booking tickets. If you want to try Claude Duet, you can get on the waitlist, though you’ll need to be a Pro or Max subscriber in the US to use it.

articles.title: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Startup Recursive has released Flint, a free, laptop-sized coding model built largely by its own AI research system, as an early test of AI that improves itself.
articles.body:
Recursive , an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint , on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI.

Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months.

Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop.

The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.

Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid the usage fees that AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes. The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open-source license that allows free use and modification.

Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time. That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open , an open model built for Macs that was released last week. Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory.

Flint is also fast. In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second.

On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint.

The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants, and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps. Still, early reviews were positive. Wired’s Will Knight used Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research. He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time.

The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments and uses the results to decide what to try next. According to the company’s launch video , it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pre-training to post-training and inference.

Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations.

Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research. OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher.

If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help. The company previously told TechCrunch that its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.”

The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong. Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster.

articles.title: Meta to create a new class of shares to fund AI push
articles.summary: Meta is creating a new class of shares to fund its AI initiatives as it pours billions into the industry.
articles.body: Meta says it’s issuing a new class of shares to fund its AI initiatives. As part of its third-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday, the company says the non-voting stock will also go toward potential acquisitions and employee compensation, with trading beginning in 2027. “The scale of investment required to compete, sustain growth, expand infrastructure, and pursue new strategic initiatives amidst the AI transformation taking place in the industry is significant,” Meta says in the press release. Susan Li, Meta’s chief financial officer, added during an earnings call that the new class of shares will “expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI.” Meta has poured billions of dollars into the AI race as it builds (and promotes) sprawling data centers, poaches top talent from other companies like OpenAI, and builds AI models capable of rivaling those from other tech giants. The company expects capital expenditures between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, up from the previous $130 billion and $145 billion estimate. It’s been a busy past few weeks for Meta, which launched its AI agent, Muse, in September. Like other AI agents, Muse can do things like clean out your email inbox, book restaurant reservations, and plan trips. The Muse app shot to the top of app stores shortly after its rollout, and hit 10 million downloads in the US this week. Meta also rolled out its Muse Wonder model this week. Muse’s launch hasn’t come without some snags. Amid concerns about user privacy, a tech YouTuber reported that the agent gave out his address to a stranger on Facebook Marketplace. The company has also had to pause Muse’s conversation-sharing feature after researchers discovered chats publicly available on the web.

articles.title: Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains
articles.summary: In just five years, pollution stemming from data centers’ electricity demand could wipe out decades of gains in air quality.
articles.body: A rush of new data centers could bring air pollution roaring back to levels not seen since the 2000s in Texas, which has become ground zero for the physical infrastructure behind generative AI. New and proposed data centers are demanding a tremendous amount of electricity. How developers and utilities meet that demand — with gas turbines or renewable energy — will determine just how dirty things will get. So far, though, things are looking grim. Tech companies and data center developers are devising new ways to get enough electricity, including building out their own power sources. But if all planned data center projects were to plug into the electricity grid in Texas and be powered by the anticipated grid mix, soot and smog-forming pollutants would skyrocket, according to a new report from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). In just five years, it would be enough pollution to wipe out decades of gains in air quality. In that scenario, fine particle pollution or soot from the power sector would more than triple, reaching its highest level since 2006. Smog-forming NOx emissions would increase 136 percent, approaching pollution levels from 2004. Planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution would climb 90 percent above what they were in 2025. That’s not set in stone, of course. HARC modeled different outcomes based on three different projections for data center energy demand. Many proposed data center projects are speculative and could fall by the wayside. And developers can limit the environmental impact of a data center by building solar and wind farms onsite. NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower if data centers pair grid power with renewable electricity generated onsite. But if developers decide to build gas engines on site to power their data centers as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to the grid, the opposite could also play out, resulting in the highest pollution levels possible. Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power they draw, and Texas has become the leading data center market in this measure with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. Texas is also bracing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on power generated onsite than any other state, according to a separate Wood Mackenzie report published in March. And in many cases, developers are turning to less efficient gas turbine technology in order to speed construction — another trend that’s making the data center boom more polluting than it needs to be. “There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” John Hall, HARC CEO, said in a press release. “The transportation sector, the state, and other stakeholders have been working for decades to successfully bring these [emissions] numbers down, and that progress is now at risk.”

articles.title: Meta wants to pay for its broad AI buildout with a newly created class of stock | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The social media giant is planning a new stock strategy to help power its broad investments in AI models and services.
articles.body:
Meta is making a big push into AI, and it’s creating a new kind of stock that could help pay for it.

On Wednesday, as the company reported its third-quarter earnings, Semafor reported the company might issue non-voting stock, meaning shares that don’t give their owners a vote on company decisions, to help fund its push into artificial intelligence.

During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting. Meta’s chief financial officer, Susan Li, said the company plans to “create a new class of non-voting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders through a stock dividend.”

Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.”

The shares will allow the company to maintain its current “founder-led structure,” she added. They will also expand its “funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI.”

Meta’s earnings were strong this past quarter, beating Wall Street expectations. The company made $64 billion in revenue, a jump of 26% from a year earlier. Its costs and expenses also rose too, however, by 68% year over year.

Reality Labs, the division responsible for Meta’s AR glasses, VR headsets, and VR software, continues to lose money, though less than it used to. The company said in its earnings report that it expects the division’s losses to shrink from its 2025 levels to between $18 billion and $19 billion.

Meta has made a big push into AI over the past year. The company has released several AI models, including Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer earlier this year. In recent weeks, it added Muse Wonder and Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model whose underlying parameters are publicly available for outsiders to use and build on. Meta also launched a coding agent for software developers called Muse Code. At its Meta Connect event this year, the company announced a new line of cute and cuddly avatars for AI assistant, Meta Muse, in a push to make its AI services more relatable (and also meme-able ).

As far as can be discerned, those AI products are doing well. “In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada have set up Muse personal agents,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s earnings call. “Growth continues to be strong, and we have been number one in the App Store almost every day.”

“Now that Muse has clear product-market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it,” Zuckerberg added, claiming later that the company expects to grow the product’s appeal to eventually “serve billions of people.”

The company also noted that certain storm clouds linger on the horizon in the form of ongoing regulatory and legal issues. “We continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” said Li. “For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets, and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States.”

articles.title: Blackstone’s Jas Khaira says fears over AI-buildout debt are overblown
articles.summary: Blackstone’s AI head on why the PE giant isn't panicked by market jitters.
articles.body:
Private equity giant Blackstone is putting itself at the center of the AI boom, firm veteran Jas Khaira discussed last week on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

It is writing checks via various strategies, ranging from offering massive loans to data centers to investing in frontier AI models and applications.

Earlier this year, the firm launched Blackstone N1 (BXN1), a San Francisco-based central hub for its AI initiatives. The group is led by Khaira, who relocated from New York to be at the epicenter of AI.

Unlike earlier tech cycles such as mobile or SaaS, which allowed companies to reach significant scale with moderate capital, the transition to AI requires staggering amounts of investment. That need for capital is precisely why Blackstone, with its $1.3 trillion in assets under management, could play such a critical role in this tech shift.

Khaira emphasized that Blackstone sets itself apart from traditional venture capitalists through its focus on compute financing and its ability to offer flexible capital structures, ranging from debt to equity. And it has been investing aggressively.

“We’re the largest owner of compute outside of the hyperscalers today, whether it’s investments in neo clouds, investments in data centers, and being able to use that compute strategically to support companies,” Khaira said.

For instance, BXN1 played a key role in several compute-related deals, among them Crux AI, a neocloud launched in partnership with Google to commercialize its custom TPUs, to which Blackstone committed $5 billion as an investor. It also backed four-year-old Etched , a chip startup whose rapid development has caught investor attention. Neoclouds are cloud providers that rent out AI GPU infrastructure.

Blackstone pioneered a financing structure that allowed it to lend massive sums to venture-backed cloud neoclouds by analyzing both committed customer contracts and using GPUs pledged as collateral.

Blackstone’s first such deal came in 2023 with CoreWeave, shortly after that neocloud saw demand explode following the launch of ChatGPT. Despite having only “30 million of revenue and minimal profitability” at that time, according to Khaira, CoreWeave approached Blackstone for a $2.3 billion loan.

CoreWeave was borrowing against the considerable value of its large collection of Nvidia GPUs, with Nvidia also an investor. Blackstone also grew more comfortable with the loan because CoreWeave had contracts with blue-chip customers like Microsoft.

That transaction quickly became the financing model for how Blackstone and other credit institutions provided billions in follow-on debt to CoreWeave and rival neoclouds.

“One of the primary things that we’re looking to is the nature of the customer. And if the customer is an investment-grade customer — let’s say it’s Microsoft or let’s say it’s Meta — the risk gets priced relative to that customer,” Khaira said.

Building on its success with CoreWeave, Blackstone struck other neocloud financing deals, including co-leading alongside Coatue a $10 billion credit facility for Australian GPU provider Firmus earlier this year.

Khaira acknowledged that in recent weeks, the large debt burdens accumulated by these companies and other neocloud operators have begun to raise red flags. Coreweave’s debt alone has since ballooned to about $50 billion , causing Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner to note in a recent CNBC interview, “The collateral that CoreWeave is putting up which is really only GPUs is not good enough anymore. They used that in the past to get cheap debt.”

Khaira said that on the credit side, the market jitters stem from a combination of factors. Interest rates ticked up in September, and hotter-than-expected inflation signals that borrowing costs may keep climbing. The flood of AI infrastructure debt offerings isn’t helping either.

“We’re also seeing higher credit spreads,” Khaira said, explaining that lenders are charging higher premiums on top of already higher base interest rates to finance the AI buildout. “The cost of capital to price in debt for a Meta or a Microsoft has widened out,” he added, pointing out that even tech giants with massive balance sheets and solid earnings are paying more to borrow.

Concerns about the rising cost of debt have spilled into the stock market. Shares of CoreWeave dropped over 20% in recent days, while Firmus scrapped its planned IPO on the Australian Securities Exchange at a target valuation of roughly $30 billion.

“Ultimately, the market wasn’t there at that valuation, and so I think as a result, that deal didn’t get done,” Khaira said about Firmus’ cancelled listing.

“The market is thinking what is the right price for neoclouds, what is the right price for these businesses in this moment when interest rates are moving up,” he said.

Despite those pressures on some infrastructure providers, AI companies simply can’t get enough compute to power their models. Their appetite continues to drive data center buildout.

Khaira downplayed worries of doom-mongers that the massive accumulation of AI infrastructure debt could lead to a widespread credit crisis, or worse, crash the economy altogether. “This doesn’t feel like something where you’ve got 2008 banks that are shaky credits,” he said.

Instead, he pointed out that because the vast majority of data centers are built for hyperscalers, the debt financing them is ultimately backed “by the most creditworthy companies in the world.”

Beyond funding data centers, Blackstone is helping companies adopt AI through a $1.5 billion joint venture called “Ode with Anthropic,” formed alongside Anthropic and Hellman & Friedman this year. Ode supplies forward-deployed engineers to help companies adopt AI and integrate it into their operations, starting with Blackstone’s 280 portfolio companies.

When asked if Blackstone-owned companies are seeing tangible gains from AI, Khaira conceded that “there is definitely ROI, but it is uneven.” He described technology adoption as something that could move in a “sawtooth-type pattern,” which, to skeptics, can look like an oversupply of compute before adoption catches up.

articles.title: Anthropic introduces Claude Duet AI agent app for professionals: Features, availability and more
articles.summary: Anthropic has introduced Claude Duet, a new AI-powered app designed to help professionals and small business owners manage their work with less manual
articles.body: Anthropic has introduced Claude Duet, a new AI-powered app designed to help professionals and small business owners manage their work with less manual effort. The app can monitor connected accounts, flag tasks that need attention, prepare reports and handle work in the background, even when users step away from their devices. Unlike a chatbot that waits for instructions, Claude Duet can proactively alert users about important updates and help complete tasks across different apps. The research preview is now open through a waitlist for users in the US with Claude Pro and Max subscriptions, with access available on iOS, Android and the web.“We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track,” Anthropic said.Claude Duet: What can the new AI agent doAccording to the company, Claude Duet is designed to help users manage busy schedules and prioritise important work. Each morning, it can send a short summary of key items across connected apps. It then checks those accounts every few hours and sends notifications when something needs attention.Users can also assign tasks, ranging from scheduling meetings and drafting emails to building dashboards, preparing financial forecasts and developing web apps.The app is built around Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 model and is designed to decide which tasks need immediate attention and when it should ask users for guidance.One of the key features of Claude Duet is its ability to continue working when users are away from their phones or computers. The app uses a virtual machine with its own browser to carry out tasks in the background. Users can send instructions through text or voice in a single ongoing conversation and receive a notification when a task is complete or requires their review.Claude Duet also carries over existing memory, skills and connected apps from a user's Claude account, which Anthropic says should make setup easier.Anthropic says Claude Duet is designed to ask for permission before taking important actions on a user's behalf. The app can read messages, draft replies and prepare work independently. However, it must seek approval before sending messages, making payments, signing documents or deleting anything.Some actions, such as trading securities or transferring money between accounts, are not allowed even with user approval.The company has also introduced additional safeguards to protect sensitive information. According to Anthropic, the system is designed to block requests to share highly sensitive details, such as credit card numbers and government identification. Other sensitive information, including health and personal financial details, can be shared only when users have explicitly instructed the app to do so.Claude Duet supports thousands of business toolsClaude Duet can connect with more than 6,000 connectors and plugins through the Claude Marketplace, allowing it to work with tools used by businesses. These integrations can help users find missed messages in Gmail and Slack, track unpaid invoices through QuickBooks or Stripe, prepare payroll in Gusto, draft job postings for LinkedIn and manage customer information in HubSpot.It can also help businesses create marketing campaigns using Canva and manage Shopify stores. Anthropic says support for a richer visual editor for Shopify storefronts is coming soon.Users can also make business purchases through Link, Stripe's digital wallet, and use Shop Pay for online checkout. Support for signing in to websites through saved 1Password logins is planned for a future update.Claude Duet availability and subscription detailsAnthropic has opened a research preview of Claude Duet through a waitlist, starting with Claude Pro and Max subscribers in the US. The app is available as a standalone offering on iOS and Android, as well as through claude.ai.During the preview, Claude Duet shares the same usage limits as the user's existing Claude plan. Background checks and complex tasks can consume those limits more quickly than ordinary conversations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
